title: Lesson 14: The Human-in-the-Loop Supervision Bar for Your Org
description: Grounded in Lesson 14 of the AI Adoption series: why a blanket 'review everything' rule fails, the difference between human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, and human-in-command, how to set a risk-based supervision bar, and why automation bias undermines reviews.

questions.question: Lesson 14 opens by arguing that telling the team to review every piece of AI output is the most common oversight mistake. Why does the blanket 'review everything' instruction fail?
options: Because it makes people review less often out of defiance
Because it covers everything without sorting what matters, so attention flattens and the outputs that genuinely need care get the same glance as the rest
Because it is too hard for most employees to remember
Because reviewing every output slows the system down past the point of usefulness
questions.explanation: Lesson 14 explains that when every output is a mandatory review, the reviews blur and stop being decisions, so the outputs that genuinely need care get exactly the same attention as the ones that do not. The fix is a supervision bar that sorts AI work into categories and names the ones that require a real, owned human decision.

questions.question: Lesson 14 defines three ways humans relate to an AI system. Which configuration is the right fit for an irreversible, high-consequence decision such as final customer pricing?
options: Human-in-the-loop: a named person must approve the output before the workflow proceeds
Human-on-the-loop: the system runs and a person supervises from above, stepping in only on anomalies
Human-in-command only, with no daily involvement at all
No human involvement, because the system's accuracy makes review unnecessary
questions.explanation: Lesson 14 sets the bar by consequence and reversibility. High-consequence or hard-to-reverse work sits below the bar and needs human-in-the-loop: a named person must sign off before release. Human-on-the-loop fits routine, reversible, low-impact work where catching the occasional anomaly is enough.

questions.question: The EU AI Act's human oversight article lists capabilities an overseeing person must have. Lesson 14 also names automation bias as a supervision failure. Which of these is the practical design lesson the lesson draws from that list?
options: Putting a named human in the loop is sufficient, even if they lack authority
The reviewer must understand the system, monitor for anomalies, know the over-reliance risk, interpret output, and be able to override or stop it, so supervisor authority must be real, not ceremonial
Reviews should focus on the lowest-risk outputs so errors are caught early
Supervision is only about speed, so reviewers should approve as fast as possible
questions.explanation: Lesson 14 reads the EU AI Act's human oversight list backward as a design requirement: a person cannot oversee a system they do not understand, they slide into over-reliance when output is usually right, and if they cannot override or stop the system they are a notary, not an overseer. So the supervision bar must guarantee these capabilities and give the reviewer real authority.
